citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

**Second-order space.** Define
$H^2(I):=\{u\in H^1(I):Du\in H^1(I)\},$
and for $u\in H^2(I)$ write $D^2u:=D(Du)\in L^2(I;\mathbb C)$; the norm is
$\|u\|_{H^2}=(\|u\|_{L^2}^2+\|Du\|_{L^2}^2+\|D^2u\|_{L^2}^2)^{1/2}$.
Thus $H^2(I)$ consists exactly of the classes in $L^2(I)$ whose first and
second weak derivatives exist and lie in $L^2(I)$, and $H^2(I)\subseteq
H^1(I)$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[def-countable-choice]]). Let $u^*$ denote the continuous absolutely
continuous representative of a class in $H^1$ supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-intervals-weak-derivative-ac-representative]], and write
$\|u\|=\|u\|_{L^2}$ and $\|u'\|=\|u'\|_{L^2}$ for the norms of
[[def-nrqm-intervals-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]] on the interval under
consideration.

(b) *Endpoint-vanishing space.* $H^1_0(0,L)=\{u\in H^1(0,L):u^*(0)=u^*(L)=0\}$,
with the traces $u^*(0),u^*(L)$ of the continuous representative.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.
Then $T$ is closable if and only if $D(T^*)$ is dense in $H$. In that case
$\overline T=T^{**}$ and $T^*=\overline T^{\,*}$; moreover if $T\subseteq T^*$,
then $T$ is closable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim:
Density follows from [F3]. For $f,g\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$, integration by
parts gives $\langle -f'',g\rangle=\langle f,-g''\rangle$, since both
functions and their derivatives vanish near the endpoints. Thus $T_c$ is
dense and symmetric.

Suppose $u\in L^2(0,L)$ has distributional second derivative
$D^2u=h\in L^2(0,L)$. By [F6], $h\in L^1(0,L)$. Define
$v(x)=\int_0^x h(t)\,dt$. Then $|v(x)|\le\|h\|_{L^1}\le\sqrt L\|h\|_2$,
so $v\in L^2(0,L)$. For every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$, choose a
measurable representative of $h$ and define
$$G(t,x):=\mathbf 1_{\{0<t<x<L\}}h(t)\varphi'(x),\qquad (t,x)\in(0,L)^2.$$
The function $q(t,x)=|h(t)||\varphi'(x)|$ is nonnegative and
product-measurable. By [F6], $h\in L^1(0,L)$. The test derivative
$\varphi'$ is continuous with compact support in $(0,L)$, hence belongs to
$L^2(0,L)$; [F6] then gives $\varphi'\in L^1(0,L)$. Tonelli [F8], applied only to
this nonnegative product, gives
$$\int_{(0,L)^2}q\,d(\lambda\times\lambda)=\left(\int_0^L|h(t)|\,dt\right)\left(\int_0^L|\varphi'(x)|\,dx\right)<\infty.$$
Since $|G|\le q$, this establishes $G\in L^1((0,L)^2)$ without using
Fubini to prove its own hypothesis. Its sections are integrable for every
parameter because $h,\varphi'\in L^1(0,L)$. Fubini [F9] therefore gives
$$\int_0^L v(x)\varphi'(x)\,dx=\int_0^L\int_0^x h(t)\varphi'(x)\,dt\,dx=\int_0^Lh(t)\left(\int_t^L\varphi'(x)\,dx\right)dt=-\int_0^Lh(t)\varphi(t)\,dt,$$
where [F7] applied to real and imaginary parts gives
$\int_t^L\varphi'(x)\,dx=\varphi(L)-\varphi(t)=-\varphi(t)$, since
$\varphi$ vanishes near $L$. Hence $Dv=h$ weakly and $v\in H^1$.
The distribution $Du-v$ has derivative zero. For every test function
$\varphi$ of integral zero, its primitive
$\psi(x)=\int_0^x\varphi(t)\,dt$ is compactly supported in $(0,L)$, and hence
$(Du-v)(\varphi)=(Du-v)(D\psi)=-(D(Du-v))(\psi)=0$. Obtain a test
function $\eta$ with integral one as follows. The constant function $1$ lies
in $L^2(0,L)$ with norm $\sqrt L$. By the density in [F3], choose
$\chi\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$ with $\|\chi-1\|_2<\sqrt L/2$; then
$\|\chi\|_2>\sqrt L/2$. Set $\eta=|\chi|^2/\|\chi\|_2^2$. It is a smooth
compactly supported test function and $\int_0^L\eta=1$. For arbitrary
$\varphi$,
$\varphi-(\int_0^L\varphi)\eta$ has integral zero, so
$(Du-v)(\varphi)=(Du-v)(\eta)\int_0^L\varphi$. Therefore $Du-v$ is a constant
distribution, $Du=v+c\in L^2$, and $u\in H^2(0,L)$ by [F1].

If $g\in H^2(0,L)$, [F2] applied with a compactly supported test function
shows $\langle T_cf,g\rangle=\langle f,-D^2g\rangle$; thus
$g\in D(T_c^*)$ and $T_c^*g=-D^2g$. Conversely, if $g\in D(T_c^*)$ and
$h=T_c^*g$, testing the adjoint identity against every
$f\in C_c^\infty(0,L)$ gives distributionally $D^2g=-h\in L^2$. Step 1.2
then gives $g\in H^2(0,L)$. Hence $T_c^*=T_{\max}$ with exactly the claimed
domain.

By [F5] and step 2.1, $T_{\min}=T_c^{**}=T_{\max}^*$. If
$u\in D(T_{\max}^*)$ and $h=T_{\max}^*u$, testing against
$C_c^\infty(0,L)\subset H^2(0,L)$ gives distributionally $D^2u=-h$.
Step 1.2 implies $u\in H^2(0,L)$. The adjoint identity for all
$g\in H^2(0,L)$ and [F2] now reads
$\langle\Gamma_1g,\Gamma_0u\rangle-\langle\Gamma_0g,\Gamma_1u\rangle=0$.
By step 1.3 the two traces of $g$ can be prescribed independently: first set
$\Gamma_0g=0$ and vary $\Gamma_1g$ to obtain $\Gamma_0u=0$; then set
$\Gamma_1g=0$ and vary $\Gamma_0g$ to obtain $\Gamma_1u=0$. Conversely, if
$u\in H^2$ has both traces zero, [F2] gives
$\langle T_{\max}g,u\rangle=\langle g,-D^2u\rangle$ for every
$g\in H^2$, so $u\in D(T_{\max}^*)$. Therefore
$D(T_{\min})=\{u\in H^2:\Gamma_0u=\Gamma_1u=0\}$ and its action is
$-D^2u$.

The preceding steps establish density, symmetry, the exact adjoint, the
closure domain, and trace surjectivity as stated.

citations.quote:
> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Fix a positive scalar $E_*$ and write $I_H$ for the identity on $H$. The
**scaled deficiency subspaces** of $S$ at $E_*$ are
$N_+(S;E_*):=\ker(S^*-iE_*I_H)$ and
$N_-(S;E_*):=\ker(S^*+iE_*I_H)$. Their **deficiency indices** are
$n_\pm(S;E_*):=\dim N_\pm(S;E_*)$, where Hilbert dimension means the
cardinality of an orthonormal basis as in the standard deficiency-index
definition. The spaces are closed: if $g_k\in N_\pm(S;E_*)$ and $g_k\to g$,
then $S^*g_k=\pm iE_*g_k\to\pm iE_*g$, so closedness of $S^*$ gives
$g\in D(S^*)$ and $S^*g=\pm iE_*g$. The dimension convention is well defined
under Choice by the cited deficiency-index definition.

**Dimension convention and well-definedness.** An orthonormal basis exists
in each $K_\pm$ by [[thm-existence-of-a-maximal-orthonormal-family]], using
full AC. Its cardinality is independent of the basis, as follows. Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ be two orthonormal bases of the same
Hilbert space. By [[thm-bessel-inequality-for-an-arbitrary-orthonormal-family]],
for each $i$ and integer $n\ge1$ at most $n$ indices satisfy
$|\langle e_i,f_j\rangle|^2\ge1/n$. Thus the support in $J$ of each row is
countable. Each column has a nonzero entry: otherwise $f_j$ is orthogonal
to the dense span of all $e_i$, hence to itself, contradicting norm one.
Here orthogonality passes to the closure by
[[lem-orthogonal-complement-is-closed]]. If $I$ is infinite, full AC lets
us enumerate the row supports and assign each $j$ to one row containing it;
this gives an injection $J\to I\times\mathbb N$. Cardinal absorption
[[cor-cardinal-absorption]] and cardinal comparison
[[lem-cardinal-arithmetic-basic-laws]] give $|J|\le|I|$.
If $I$ has finite size $n$, the residual
$f_j-\sum_{i\in I}\langle f_j,e_i\rangle e_i$ is orthogonal to the dense
span of the $e_i$ and so vanishes. Taking its norm gives
$\sum_{i\in I}|\langle f_j,e_i\rangle|^2=1$.
For every finite $F\subseteq J$, Bessel in the other direction yields
$$|F|=\sum_{j\in F}\sum_{i\in I}|\langle f_j,e_i\rangle|^2=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in F}|\langle e_i,f_j\rangle|^2\le n.$$
Hence $|J|\le n$. Exchanging the two bases proves equality of cardinalities
in all cases. In the finite case each basis also spans algebraically by the
same residual argument, so this is the ordinary linear dimension. For the
zero space the basis is empty and the dimension is zero. AC is used for
basis existence and the simultaneous choices in the infinite comparison.

Assume Countable Choice. For a densely defined linear operator $T$ on $H$ the
adjoint $T^*$ is well defined and linear with linear domain $D(T^*)$; $T^*$ is
closed; for every $z\in\mathbb C$
$$\operatorname{ran}(T-z)^\perp=\ker(T^*-\overline z),$$
and if $S\subseteq T$ and both are densely defined, then $T^*\subseteq S^*$.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$. Then every $x\in H$ has a unique decomposition

$T$ is **closed** when $\Gamma(T)$ is a closed subset of $H\oplus H$. A linear
operator is determined by its graph, and the following elementary translations
are used silently below: $\Gamma(T)$ is a linear subspace of $H\oplus H$;
$\Gamma(T)\cap(\{0\}\oplus H)=\{(0,0)\}$; the image of $\Gamma(T)$ under the
first coordinate projection is $D(T)$; and $T\subseteq S$ if and only if
$\Gamma(T)\subseteq\Gamma(S)$. In particular a closed operator is exactly one
whose graph is a closed subspace of $H\oplus H$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a self-adjoint
operator on $H$. By
[[thm-self-adjoint-resolvent-estimate]] the points $\pm i$ lie in $\rho(T)$, so
$T+i$ and $T-i$ are bijections of $D(T)$ onto $H$ with bounded inverses, and
$$C_T:=(T-i)(T+i)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)$$
is a bounded everywhere defined operator, the **Cayley transform** of $T$. In
the resolvent convention $R_T(z)=(z-T)^{-1}$ of
[[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]] one has
$$(T+i)^{-1}=-R_T(-i),\qquad C_T=I+2iR_T(-i)=I-2i(T+i)^{-1}.$$

Assume Countable Choice. The map $T\mapsto C_T=(T-i)(T+i)^{-1}$ is a bijection
from the set of self-adjoint operators on $H$ onto the set of unitary operators
$U$ on $H$ with $\ker(I-U)=\{0\}$. The inverse map assigns to such a $U$ the
operator
$$D(T_U)=\operatorname{ran}(I-U),\qquad T_U(I-U)y=i(I+U)y\quad(y\in H).$$
For this $T_U$ both $T_U-i$ and $T_U+i$ map $D(T_U)$ onto $H$, so $T_U$ is
self-adjoint, and $C_{T_U}=U$.

**Dimension convention and well-definedness.** An orthonormal basis exists
in each $K_\pm$ by [[thm-existence-of-a-maximal-orthonormal-family]], using
full AC. Its cardinality is independent of the basis, as follows. Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ be two orthonormal bases of the same
Hilbert space. By [[thm-bessel-inequality-for-an-arbitrary-orthonormal-family]],
for each $i$ and integer $n\ge1$ at most $n$ indices satisfy

countable. Each column has a nonzero entry: otherwise $f_j$ is orthogonal

Here orthogonality passes to the closure by
[[lem-orthogonal-complement-is-closed]]. If $I$ is infinite, full AC lets
us enumerate the row supports and assign each $j$ to one row containing it;

[[cor-cardinal-absorption]] and cardinal comparison
[[lem-cardinal-arithmetic-basic-laws]] give $|J|\le|I|$.
If $I$ has finite size $n$, the residual
$f_j-\sum_{i\in I}\langle f_j,e_i\rangle e_i$ is orthogonal to the dense
span of the $e_i$ and so vanishes. Taking its norm gives
$\sum_{i\in I}|\langle f_j,e_i\rangle|^2=1$.
For every finite $F\subseteq J$, Bessel in the other direction yields
$$|F|=\sum_{j\in F}\sum_{i\in I}|\langle f_j,e_i\rangle|^2=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in F}|\langle e_i,f_j\rangle|^2\le n.$$
Hence $|J|\le n$. Exchanging the two bases proves equality of cardinalities
in all cases. In the finite case each basis also spans algebraically by the

Let $A$ and $B$ be sets and let $f : A \to B$ be a function ([[def-function]]).

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

derivations.claim:
The graph of $A$ is the image of the graph of $S$ under the bounded
invertible map $(f,g)\mapsto(f,E_*^{-1}g)$ on $H\oplus H$, so it is closed;
real scaling preserves symmetry. If $g\in D(S^*)$, then for every
$f\in D(S)$,
$\langle Af,g\rangle=E_*^{-1}\langle Sf,g\rangle
=\langle f,E_*^{-1}S^*g\rangle$, so $g\in D(A^*)$ and
$A^*g=E_*^{-1}S^*g$. Conversely, if $g\in D(A^*)$, then
$\langle Sf,g\rangle=E_*\langle Af,g\rangle
=\langle f,E_*A^*g\rangle$, so $g\in D(S^*)$ and
$S^*g=E_*A^*g$. Therefore $D(A^*)=D(S^*)$ and
$A^*=E_*^{-1}S^*$. Since
$A^*\mp iI=E_*^{-1}(S^*\mp iE_*I)$, the ordinary deficiency spaces of
$A$ at $\pm i$ are exactly $N_\pm$.

Suppose $n_+=n_-$. Choose orthonormal bases $(e_j)_{j\in J_+}$ of $N_+$
and $(f_j)_{j\in J_-}$ of $N_-$. By [F6], choose a bijection
$\pi:J_+\to J_-$. The map $V_0e_j=f_{\pi(j)}$ preserves norms on finite
linear combinations by orthonormality, so it extends continuously to an
isometry $V:N_+\to N_-$. Its range contains the finite span of the $f_j$,
which is dense; the range of an isometry from the complete space $N_+$ is
closed, so $V$ is onto and unitary.

For $f\in D(A)$, symmetry makes $\langle Af,f\rangle$ real; expanding the
two norms gives
$\|(A\pm iI)f\|^2=\|Af\|^2+\|f\|^2$. Thus $A\pm iI$ are injective. If
$(A\pm iI)f_k$ converges, the norm identity applied to differences makes
$(f_k)$ Cauchy and then $(Af_k)$ Cauchy; closedness of $A$ shows the limit is
in the range. Hence $M_\pm:=\operatorname{ran}(A\pm iI)$ are closed. By [F2]
and [F3], $H=M_+\oplus N_+=M_-\oplus N_-$, with orthogonal sums.

Equip $D(A^*)$ with the graph inner product
$\langle f,g\rangle_{A^*}=\langle f,g\rangle+\langle A^*f,A^*g\rangle$.
It is complete by [F2, F4], and $D(A)$ is a closed subspace because $A$ is
closed and $A^*f=Af$ there. If $z\in D(A^*)$ is graph-orthogonal to $D(A)$,
then for every $f\in D(A)$,
$\langle Af,A^*z\rangle=-\langle f,z\rangle$. By the adjoint definition,
this means $A^*z\in D(A^*)$ and $A^{*2}z=-z$. Therefore
$z_+=(z-iA^*z)/2$ and $z_-=(z+iA^*z)/2$ satisfy
$A^*z_+=iz_+$ and $A^*z_-=-iz_-$, and $z=z_++z_-$. Conversely,
$D(A)$ is graph-orthogonal to both kernels: for $u\in N_+$,
$\langle f,u\rangle+\langle Af,A^*u\rangle
=\langle f,u\rangle+\langle Af,iu\rangle=0$ by the adjoint identity and
conjugate-linearity in the second argument, and the same computation with
$A^*u=-iu$ holds for $u\in N_-$. If $u\in N_+$ and $v\in N_-$, then
$\langle u,v\rangle+\langle A^*u,A^*v\rangle
=\langle u,v\rangle+\langle iu,-iv\rangle=0$. Thus the two kernels are
graph-orthogonal to each other. Applying [F3] in the graph Hilbert space proves the orthogonal
decomposition
$D(A^*)=D(A)\oplus N_+\oplus N_-$.

Define $C_A:M_+\to M_-$ by
$C_A((A+iI)f)=(A-iI)f$. Injectivity of $A+iI$ makes this well defined, the
norm identity in step 2.1 makes it an isometry, and it is onto $M_-$. Define
$W(m+u)=C_Am-Vu$ for $m\in M_+$ and $u\in N_+$. The decompositions from
step 2.1 make $W$ well defined; it is unitary because its two orthogonal summands
are mapped isometrically onto $M_-$ and $N_-$. For $f\in D(A)$,
$(I-W)(A+iI)f=2if$, so $\operatorname{ran}(I-W)$ is dense. If $Wz=z$, then
$z$ is orthogonal to $\operatorname{ran}(I-W)$ by unitarity, hence to the
dense domain $D(A)$, so $z=0$. The Cayley correspondence [F5] therefore gives
a self-adjoint operator $A_V$ with Cayley transform $W$.

For $m=(A+iI)f$ and $u\in N_+$, direct calculation gives
$(I-W)(m+u)=2if+u+Vu$ and
$i(I+W)(m+u)=2iAf+iu-iVu$. The Cayley inverse is
$A_V=i(I+W)(I-W)^{-1}$ on $\operatorname{ran}(I-W)$, so
$D(A_V)=\operatorname{ran}(I-W)=D(A)+\{u+Vu:u\in N_+\}$ and
$A_V(2if+u+Vu)=2iAf+iu-iVu$. Equivalently, after renaming $2if$ as $f$,
$A_V(f+u+Vu)=Af+iu-iVu$. The sum is direct: if $f=u+Vu\in D(A)$, then
$(I-W)(A+iI)f=2if=(I-W)(2iu)$; injectivity of $I-W$ gives
$(A+iI)f=2iu$. Its left side lies in $M_+$ and its right side in $N_+$,
whose intersection is zero, so $u=f=0$. Multiplication by $E_*$ gives the
displayed domain and action for $S_V=E_*A_V$. The two-way scalar-adjoint
calculation in step 1.1 applies to $A_V$ as well, so
$S_V^*=E_*A_V^*=S_V$. Thus $S_V$ is a self-adjoint
extension of $S$.

Conversely, let $T$ be any self-adjoint extension of $S$ and put
$R=E_*^{-1}T$. The two-way scalar-adjoint calculation in step 1.1 gives
$R^*=E_*^{-1}T^*=R$, so $R$ is a self-adjoint extension of $A$. Its Cayley transform $C_R$
is unitary by [F5] and agrees with $C_A$ on $M_+$, since $R$ equals $A$ on
$D(A)$. A unitary carrying $M_+$ onto $M_-$ carries their orthogonal
complements $N_+$ onto $N_-$ by step 2.1 and [F2]; hence
$C_R(N_+)=N_-$. Put $V=-C_R|_{N_+}$; this is unitary. The
unitary $W$ constructed from this $V$ agrees with $C_R$ on both orthogonal
summands of $H$, so uniqueness in [F5] gives $R=A_V$. This determines $V$
uniquely from $T$ and proves that every self-adjoint extension of $S$ is
uniquely $S_V$.

If $n_+=n_-$, step 1.2 supplies a unitary and step 4.1 supplies a
self-adjoint extension. If an extension exists, step 4.2 supplies a unitary
$N_+\to N_-$, so its orthonormal bases have bijective index sets and
$n_+=n_-$. This proves the existence equivalence and the complete
parameterization.

$$D(T_{\min})=\{f\in H^2(0,L): f(0)=f'(0)=f(L)=f'(L)=0\},$$
with $T_{\min}f=-D^2f$. The trace map
$\gamma:H^2(0,L)\to\mathbb C^4$ defined by

adjoint $T^*$ is well defined and linear with linear domain $D(T^*)$; $T^*$ is

$$\operatorname{ran}(T-z)^\perp=\ker(T^*-\overline z),$$
and if $S\subseteq T$ and both are densely defined, then $T^*\subseteq S^*$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert
space and $S:D(S)\to H$ a densely defined, closed, symmetric linear operator.
Fix $E_*>0$ and let $N_\pm=N_\pm(S;E_*)$ and
$n_\pm=\dim N_\pm$ be the scaled deficiency spaces and indices. For every
unitary map $V:N_+\to N_-$, the operator
$$D(S_V)=D(S)\oplus\{u+Vu:u\in N_+\},\qquad
S_V(f+u+Vu)=Sf+iE_*u-iE_*Vu$$
is a self-adjoint extension of $S$. Every self-adjoint extension of $S$ is
uniquely $S_V$ for one such $V$. Consequently $S$ has a self-adjoint

We write $f : A \to B$, and say $f$ is a **function from $A$ to $B$**, when $f$
is a function with $\operatorname{dom} f = A$ and
$\operatorname{ran} f \subseteq B$ (Subset $x \subseteq y$, proper subset $x \subsetneq y$, and the separation notation $\{\, z \in x : \varphi(z) \,\}$); $A$ is the
**domain** of $f$ and $B$ is a **codomain** for $f$. Equivalently
$f \subseteq A \times B$ with $\operatorname{dom} f = A$
(The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Kuratowski ordered pair $(a,b) := \{\{a\},\{a,b\}\}$).

derivations.claim:
Let $T$ be any linear operator with $T_{\min}\subseteq T\subseteq T_{\max}$.
For this proof write $\gamma_b f=(\Gamma_0f,\Gamma_1f)\in
\mathbb C^2\times\mathbb C^2$. This is the four-coordinate trace map of
[F1] with the last coordinate sign reversed, so it is onto and has kernel
$D(T_{\min})$. Its image $M:=\gamma_b(D(T))$ is a linear subspace. Since
$\ker\gamma_b=D(T_{\min})\subseteq D(T)$, every $f\in H^2$ whose trace lies
in $M$ differs from a member of $D(T)$ by an element of $D(T_{\min})$; thus
$D(T)=\gamma_b^{-1}(M)$. Conversely, every linear subspace $M$ gives such a
domain because $\gamma_b$ is onto.

Define
$B((a,b),(a',b'))=\langle b,a'\rangle-\langle a,b'\rangle$ and
$M^\omega=\{z:B(m,z)=0\text{ for every }m\in M\}$. By [F2], integration by
parts gives $T^*=T_{\gamma_b^{-1}(M^\omega)}$: indeed, since
$T_{\min}\subseteq T$, adjoint inclusion reversal puts $D(T^*)$ inside
$D(T_{\min}^*)=H^2$, and for $g\in H^2$ the adjoint identity for every
$f\in D(T)$ is exactly $B(\gamma_b f,\gamma_b g)=0$. Hence $T$ is self-adjoint
if and only if $M=M^\omega$.

Put $\gamma_\ell f=(a,b):=(\Gamma_0f,\ell\Gamma_1f)$ and let
$\widehat M=\gamma_\ell(D(T))$. Equivalently,
$\widehat M=\{(a,b):(a,b/\ell)\in M\}$, where $M$ is the unscaled trace
image from step 1.1. Define
$\widehat B((a,b),(a',b'))=\langle b,a'\rangle-\langle a,b'\rangle$ and
$\widehat M^{\widehat\omega}:=\{z:\widehat B(m,z)=0\text{ for all }m\in
\widehat M\}$.
Since $\widehat B=\ell B$ after undoing the derivative scaling and
$\ell>0$, step 1.2 gives $\widehat M=\widehat M^{\widehat\omega}$ exactly
when $T$ is self-adjoint. The map $\gamma_\ell$ is onto because the trace map
in [F1] is onto and multiplying its derivative coordinates by $\ell>0$ is
invertible. For $x=a+ib$ and $y=a-ib$, direct expansion using
the first-variable-linear inner product gives
$$\widehat B((a,b),(a',b'))=\frac{\langle x,x'\rangle-\langle y,y'\rangle}{2i}.$$
Thus $\widehat M=\widehat M^{\widehat\omega}$ implies that
$(a,b)\mapsto(x,y)$ sends $\widehat M$ to the graph of an
inner-product-preserving linear map $R:X\to\mathbb C^2$, where
$X=\{a+ib:(a,b)\in\widehat M\}$. It is well defined: if a member of
$\widehat M$ has $x=0$, isotropy gives $\|y\|^2=\|x\|^2=0$, so $y=0$.
Maximality forces
$X=\mathbb C^2$. Indeed, define $X^\perp=\{z:\langle x,z\rangle=0\text{ for every }x\in X\}$ with $\langle x,z\rangle=x_1\overline{z_1}+x_2\overline{z_2}$. Every proper complex linear subspace $X$ has a nonzero vector in $X^\perp$, by the following coordinate argument. If $X=\{0\}$, take $x_0=(1,0)$. Otherwise take $0\ne v=(v_1,v_2)\in X$. Every $w\in X$ is a multiple of $v$: if $v_1w_2-v_2w_1\ne0$, the inverse of the two-column matrix $(v,w)$ expresses both standard coordinate vectors as linear combinations of $v,w$, implying $X=\mathbb C^2$; if this determinant is zero, solving in a nonzero coordinate of $v$ gives $w=cv$. Thus for proper $X$ one has $X=\operatorname{span}\{v\}$, and $x_0=(-\overline{v_2},\overline{v_1})\ne0$ satisfies $\langle cv,x_0\rangle=c(-v_1v_2+v_2v_1)=0$. No closed-subspace decomposition or additional choice principle is used. If $X$ were proper, take this $x_0$ and set
$a=x_0/2$, $b=x_0/(2i)$, so $(x,y)=(x_0,0)$. The displayed identity makes
this boundary pair orthogonal for $\widehat B$ to all of $\widehat M$, hence it
lies in $\widehat M^{\widehat\omega}=\widehat M$; then
$x_0\in X\cap X^\perp$, a contradiction. Therefore
$R$ is a linear isometry from $\mathbb C^2$ into $\mathbb C^2$. Let
$e_1,e_2$ be the standard basis and write $Re_1=(\alpha_1,\beta_1)$ and
$Re_2=(\alpha_2,\beta_2)$. Isometry gives
$$|\alpha_1|^2+|\beta_1|^2=|\alpha_2|^2+|\beta_2|^2=1,\qquad \alpha_1\overline{\alpha_2}+\beta_1\overline{\beta_2}=0.$$
Direct expansion gives
$$|\alpha_1\beta_2-\alpha_2\beta_1|^2=(|\alpha_1|^2+|\beta_1|^2)(|\alpha_2|^2+|\beta_2|^2)-|\alpha_1\overline{\alpha_2}+\beta_1\overline{\beta_2}|^2=1.$$
Thus the matrix $U$ with columns $Re_1,Re_2$ is invertible, so these vectors
span $\mathbb C^2$ and $R$ is onto. Their orthonormality gives
$U^*U=I_2$; since $U$ is invertible, this implies $U^*=U^{-1}$ and hence
$UU^*=I_2$. Thus $U\in U(2)$, and its graph condition is
$U(a+ib)=a-ib$, equivalently
$(U-I_2)a+i(U+I_2)b=0$. This $U$ is unique because its value is fixed for
every $x\in\mathbb C^2$.

Conversely, let $U\in U(2)$ and set
$\widehat M_U=\{(a,b):U(a+ib)=a-ib\}$ in the scaled boundary coordinates.
Every $x\in\mathbb C^2$ occurs, by taking
$a=(x+Ux)/2$ and $b=(x-Ux)/(2i)$. Unitarity gives
$\langle x,x'\rangle=\langle Ux,Ux'\rangle$ for every pair, so the
displayed formula in step 2.1 makes $\widehat M_U$ isotropic. If
$(a,b)\in\widehat M_U^{\widehat\omega}$,
then for every $x'\in\mathbb C^2$ that formula gives
$\langle x',x\rangle=\langle Ux',y\rangle=\langle x',U^*y\rangle$, hence
$x=U^*y$ and $y=Ux$; therefore $(a,b)\in\widehat M_U$. Thus
$\widehat M_U=\widehat M_U^{\widehat\omega}$. Since $\gamma_\ell$ is onto,
the restriction to $\gamma_\ell^{-1}(\widehat M_U)$ is self-adjoint by the
criterion in step 1.2 and the scaling equivalence in step 2.1. Its boundary equation is exactly
the Statement's equation, and its domain lies between $T_{\min}$ and
$T_{\max}$ because it is a restriction of $T_{\max}$ whose domain contains
the zero-trace domain.

The preceding steps give a bijection from $U(2)$ to the entire set of
self-adjoint extensions between $T_{\min}$ and $T_{\max}$. By [F4], that same
extension set is uniquely parameterized by the abstract unitaries between
the deficiency subspaces. Composing the two bijections identifies the
boundary-matrix labels with the abstract deficiency labels and proves that
the displayed boundary family is exhaustive.

indices $(n_+,n_-)=(1,0)$ at reference scale $E_*=1$, and therefore has no

A **strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group** on the complex Hilbert
space $H$ is a map $U:\mathbb R\to\mathcal B(H)$ such that
$U(0)=I$, $U(s+t)=U(s)U(t)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$, each $U(t)$ is unitary
(that is, onto and norm preserving, equivalently $U(t)^*U(t)=U(t)U(t)^*=I$,
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-operator-norm]]), and the orbit maps
$t\mapsto U(t)x$ are continuous at every $t$ for every $x\in H$, from the
usual metric on $\mathbb R$ to the norm metric of $H$
([[def-metric-continuity]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The map $T\mapsto U(t)=e^{itT}$, computed by the
Borel functional calculus of $T$
([[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]]), is a bijection from the set of
self-adjoint operators on $H$ onto the set of strongly continuous
one-parameter unitary groups on $H$. Its inverse assigns to $U$ its generator
$G$ and the self-adjoint operator $T=-iG$; here $D(T)=D(G)$ is exactly the set
of vectors at which $t\mapsto U(t)x$ is differentiable at $0$, and
$\frac1t(U(t)x-x)\to iTx$ for $x\in D(T)$.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.
